title: Booking jobs in front of Werlein's and the Presidents' Ball
summary: Musicians book spot jobs at Werlein's counter; Kelly plays with Gimelli and Pete Lesseps, explains the Presidents' Ball, and becomes assistant manager.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Could be wrong, could have been. Johnny possibly played with everybody in the room. Any number of bands, because he lived down there for a long period. He finally went to California. So Johnny, of course, helped me. I worked at Warlands. I got to meet all these musicians around New Orleans. All the jobs were booked down in front of Warlands. They weren't booked at the Union or any place. I was booked in front of Warlands. In fact, police used to have to make the guys, they would be so thick, in front of 605, Canal Street. The cops would very often say, move on, move on. Customers can't get in there. But anyway, these guys would book spot jobs. And that's when I got started. They would come up to the counter and I was, they knew I played. You got a job Friday night? I said, no, I don't like a job. Okay, I want you. So, I really got lots of jobs. I played with little non-union bands like Gimelli, Joe Gimelli, I don't know if you know, I'm Angelo Gimelli, and played a lot with Pete B. Lesseps, who was a very successful agent and an orchestra leader in the Warlands. We worked in the bank. All these guys were, they were sidelining people too. But we played lots of jobs. I remember one time playing a job over at the St. Charles, which was called the President's of the National League of the War. I don't know if you've heard of this before, but at that time, during the Depression, bands would invite all of the presidents of the various social clubs to a dance. And even these two or three bands who went in on it would pay for the expense of the ballroom, refreshments, and everything, so that they had an opportunity to show how they could play and book dates. Now this is something in New Orleans history, I don't know if you've been told, but it was
No, I've never heard of this. President's Ball.

I mean, the presence of fraternities, carnival clubs, and various other organizations, and it would be quite a big thing. And so they got a lot of this engagement, and they sounded like it. So I played, I actually played with over 200 different New Orleans musicians, and I had the names of practically all of them. I just remembered them through the years, and I wrote them down after I left down there, because I knew I liked them and had so much fun with them. But when my fortunes improved, after a while, one of the fellows who was assistant manager of the department, got in some trouble with the company, and so they had to let him go. And so Mr. LaCrosse made me assistant manager of the department. And then I went on a salary, which was $25 a week and 2% of sales. Now remember, this is 1932, when I could go directly across the street from 327 Brooklyn and get a wonderful meal for 15 cents. That's actually cool.
